title: Epistola 'De Discrictione Monachorum Et Ruina Monasteriorum'
author: Eutropius Episcopus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1313.tmp1313.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Quia quod Deus bene, sancte et perfecte a sanctis et perfectis viris in hae cella sua instituit, et nunc us- que teneri voluit, nullo modo nunc propter paucos et tepidos, aut vagos et pseudomonachos, qui diver- sorum quotidie circumeunt domos, et cum Epicuro laetanter dicunt : Manducemus et bibamus, cras enim moriemur (IsaiXXII, 13), in aliquo transgredi pote- rit, aut immutari, aut dimitti. Quia, ut sanctus ait Apostolus : Firmum Dei fundamentum stat (II Tim. II, 19), etiamsi sit, qui io illo malae voluntatis suae vitio offendat et cadat, nec in aliquo vacillet aut nutet quod Deus omnipotens ana dextera protegit et con fortat.
passages.english: For what God has well, holily and perfectly instituted in this his cell through holy and perfect men, and has willed to be kept until now, can in no way now, on account of a few lukewarm men, or wandering men and false monks, who go round the houses of various people every day and say gladly with Epicurus, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die" (Isaiah 22:13), be transgressed in any respect, or changed, or abandoned. For, as the holy Apostle says, "God's firm foundation stands" (2 Timothy 2:19), even if there is someone who stumbles on it through the fault of his own evil will and falls; nor does what almighty God protects and strengthens with his right hand waver or totter in any respect.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'hae' read as 'hac', 'io illo' as 'in illo', 'ana dextera' as 'sua dextera' ("his right hand"), 'IsaiXXII' as Isaiah 22. The quotation 'Let us eat and drink...' is from Isaiah, though the author attributes the sentiment to Epicurus. The title's 'Discrictione' is probably a misprint for 'Districtione' (strictness).
